analysis.one_liner: Creates an independent FDA center to monitor drug safety after approval, order safety studies, and fine companies that don't comply.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan drug-safety bill with a Republican lead sponsor and seven cosponsors was referred to committee and never received a hearing or vote before the Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have built a new office inside the Food and Drug Administration, separate from the office that approves drugs, whose whole job is watching drugs after they reach the market. It could order companies to run safety studies, force public disclosure of study results and safety risks, restrict misleading advertising, impose fines that double every 30 days a company ignores an order, and quickly pull a drug off the market if it turns out to be dangerous. It was introduced in the aftermath of the Vioxx withdrawal, when the safety of already-approved drugs was under national scrutiny, and it sat in committee without ever getting a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients and their families, who would learn sooner when an approved drug shows signs of danger. Doctors and pharmacists would get timelier safety information through required public postings every 90 days. The FDA itself would gain a dedicated postmarket office reporting directly to the Commissioner, with staff funding authorized at $50 million rising to $150 million a year.

how_it_helps.text: Establishes a Center for Postmarket Drug Evaluation and Research inside the FDA, reporting directly to the Commissioner and separate from the office that approves drugs, to conduct ongoing risk assessment and surveillance of approved drugs and biologics.

Lets the FDA require drug companies to complete postmarket safety studies by dates and on terms the agency sets, and to contract with patient-database holders for epidemiologic studies when companies do not.

Requires the agency to publish study requirements, progress reports, results, and any risk determinations in the Federal Register and online at least every 90 days, so safety information reaches doctors and patients directly.

Authorizes civil penalties starting at $250,000 and doubling every 30 days a company fails to complete a required study or obey a corrective order, up to $2 million per 30-day period, and gives the agency expedited procedures to suspend or withdraw a dangerous drug's approval.

Requires prominent risk disclosures in a risky drug's advertising and, for the first two years after any approval, statements that not all side effects may yet be known — with ads submitted to the FDA 30 days before use.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug makers bear the cost: mandatory safety studies, fines for missed deadlines and ignored orders, mandatory advertising disclosures and pre-review, and the risk of restricted distribution or quick withdrawal of a product's approval. Taxpayers fund the new center through appropriations authorized at $50–150 million a year.

drawbacks.text: The penalty structure is modest for large companies — capped at $2 million per 30-day period — which a candid supporter would acknowledge may be too small to change behavior at major manufacturers.

Separating postmarket review into its own center, independent of the office that approves drugs, risks internal friction and slower, more duplicative decisions inside the FDA; the bill tries to manage this by requiring consultation between the two offices before ordering studies or corrective actions.

Broad corrective-action powers — including patient consent forms, distribution restrictions, and mandatory registries — could limit some patients' access to medicines they rely on, which the bill addresses by requiring the director to weigh the benefit-to-risk profile and the effect on patients who depend on the drug before acting.
Companies bear compliance costs — studies, registries, advertising review — that can ultimately be passed into drug prices.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill traded real compliance costs for a much stronger safety net around already-approved medicines, which is where drug dangers like Vioxx's surfaced. The strongest objections — small fines and possible bureaucratic friction between the new center and existing FDA offices — are genuine but do not outweigh the public-information requirements, mandatory studies, and expedited withdrawal authority for patients. It was a broad, serious bill whose main cost fell on the industry it regulated.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced with bipartisan support and referred to the Senate health committee, which never took it up — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Chuck Grassley, a Republican, introduced the bill on April 27, 2005 together with Senator Christopher Dodd, a Democrat.
Seven senators — five Democrats and two Republicans — signed on as cosponsors.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions on the day it was introduced.
No further action was ever taken: the committee held no hearing or markup, the bill never reached the floor, and the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007 with the bill dead in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Drug makers were better off: they avoided mandatory postmarket studies, escalating fines, advertising pre-review, and expedited withdrawal authority. Patients went without the stronger postmarket safety system for the rest of the decade.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Drug makers avoided stricter safety oversight

for.name: Chuck Grassley
for.role: U.S. Senator from Iowa; lead sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and pressed for a standalone postmarket drug safety center with enforcement powers.

against.name: Mike Enzi
against.role: Chair, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill; it received no action after referral.

against.name: Pharmaceutical industry
against.role: Brand-name drug manufacturers and their trade association
against.what_they_did: Opposed independent postmarket drug safety oversight and civil penalties of the kind the bill proposed during the 2005–2007 drug safety debate.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's sponsorship was bipartisan from the start — a Republican lead sponsor joined by a Democratic co-introducer and seven cosponsors split five Democrats to two Republicans — so its death in committee was not a party-line defeat.

industries.note: The bill would have required companies to run safety studies on deadlines set by the FDA, publish safety information, submit ads for review, and face escalating civil penalties up to $2 million per 30-day period — plus expedited withdrawal of a dangerous drug's approval. Its interests in this bill ran against the patients the oversight was meant to protect, since faster warnings and restrictions cut into sales of a risky product.

The bill imposed no new requirements on devices; it only required a government report identifying deficiencies in postmarket device surveillance and recommending improvements. Device makers' interest ran alongside patients' interest in better safety monitoring, though the report could have set the stage for future regulation.
